section.title: Overseers and Deacons
section.sectionRationale: Paul sets out the character required of those who lead and serve in God's household: overseers and deacons. The lists are dominated by tested character rather than talent. He then names why such order matters: the church is the household of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth, whose confession is the great mystery of godliness, God manifest in the flesh.
section.thesis: Leadership in God's household rests on proven, godly character, because the church is the pillar of the truth, and that truth is the great mystery of godliness: Christ appeared in the flesh, was vindicated, and was taken up in glory.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the qualifications for overseers; the qualifications for deacons, and the women who serve; and the reason for it all, the church as pillar of the truth confessing the mystery of godliness in Christ.

units.label: Qualifications for overseers
units.note: above reproach and able to teach

verses.text: This is a trustworthy saying: If anyone aspires to be an {{episkopos|overseer}}, he desires a noble task.
An overseer, then, must be {{anepilemptos|above reproach}}, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, {{didaktikos|able to teach}},
not dependent on wine, not violent but gentle, peaceable, and free of the love of money.
An overseer must manage his own household well and keep his children under control, with complete dignity.
For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he care for the church of God?
He must not be a recent convert, or he may become conceited and fall under the same condemnation as the devil.
Furthermore, he must have a good reputation with outsiders, so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the snare of the devil.
{{diakonos|Deacons}} likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued or given to much wine or greedy for money.
They must hold to the {{mysterion|mystery}} of the faith with a clear conscience.
Additionally, they must first be tested. Then, if they are above reproach, let them serve as deacons.
In the same way, the women must be dignified, not slanderers, but temperate and faithful in all things.
A deacon must be the husband of but one wife, a good manager of his children and of his own household.
For those who have served well as deacons acquire for themselves a high standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.

units.label: The mystery of godliness
units.note: the church, pillar of the truth

verses.text: Although I hope to come to you soon, I am writing you these things
in case I am delayed, so that you will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the {{ekklesia|church}} of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.

By common confession, the mystery of {{eusebeia|godliness}} is great: He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory.

episkopos.gloss: An overseer or guardian, one who watches over and cares for the flock. In the New Testament the term overlaps with elder, describing the same office of leadership. Paul calls aspiring to it a noble task, then insists the office be filled by men of tested character.

anepilemptos.gloss: Above reproach, giving nothing that an accuser can lay hold of. It heads the qualification list and is echoed for deacons in verse 10. It does not mean sinless but of a settled, unimpeachable reputation, so that critics find no handle against the leader or the gospel.

didaktikos.gloss: Able to teach, skilled in and apt to teach. It is the one clearly functional qualification in a list otherwise about character, marking out the overseer's duty to hold and hand on sound doctrine, guarding the church from the false teachers.

diakonos.gloss: A servant or minister; here the church office of deacon. The word stresses service, care for practical needs and people. Deacons must show the same tested, dignified character as overseers, holding the faith with a clear conscience.

mysterion.gloss: A mystery, a truth once hidden but now revealed by God. Deacons hold the mystery of the faith, and verse 16 names the mystery of godliness: the once-hidden plan of salvation now made known in Christ. It is not a secret to be earned but a revelation to be confessed.

ekklesia.gloss: The assembly or church, the called-out people of God. Paul calls it the household of the living God and the pillar and foundation of the truth. The church does not create the truth but upholds and displays it, which is why its order and leaders matter so much.

eusebeia.gloss: Godliness, true reverence for God expressed in life. The mystery of godliness is the revealed truth about Christ that produces reverent living. All the qualifications and church order in this chapter serve this godliness, which is grounded in the person and work of the incarnate Son.

basic.context: Paul lists the character needed in those who lead and serve the church. Overseers must be above reproach, self-controlled, hospitable, able to teach, and good managers of their own homes. Deacons must be dignified, tested, and hold the faith with a clear conscience. Paul explains why order matters: the church is God's household and the pillar of the truth, and that truth is the great mystery of godliness, Christ revealed in the flesh and taken up in glory.
basic.hermeneutics: The qualification lists are an enduring pattern for choosing leaders, weighted toward proven character over gifting. The closing confession in verse 16 is likely an early hymn, summarizing the gospel. The whole chapter ties godly leadership to the church's task of upholding the truth about Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: An episkopos, overseer, must be anepilemptos, above reproach, and didaktikos, able to teach. A diakonos, deacon, must hold the mysterion, mystery, of the faith. The ekklesia, church, is the pillar of truth, and the mystery of eusebeia, godliness, is Christ manifest in the flesh.
basic.typology: The overseer who manages God's household points to Christ, the faithful Son over God's house. The church as pillar and foundation of the truth continues the calling of God's people to bear witness, fulfilled in the body of Christ.
basic.christ: The chapter climaxes in the person of Christ: He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed in throughout the world, and taken up in glory. This is the mystery of godliness, the whole gospel of the incarnate, risen, and ascended Lord in one confession.
basic.god: The church is the household of the living God, and its leaders are His stewards. God cares that His people are led by those whose character matches the message, and He has made His church the pillar that upholds His revealed truth in the world.
basic.crossReferences: Titus 1 gives a parallel list of overseer qualifications. Acts 6 shows the first appointment of servants to care for practical needs. Philippians 2 celebrates the same descent and exaltation of Christ confessed in verse 16.
basic.oneStory: God has always gathered His people and guarded them through appointed leaders. Here He orders His household so it can uphold the truth about His Son. The mystery of godliness, Christ revealed and exalted, is the truth the church exists to hold high, part of God's long work of making Himself known through Jesus.

context.literary:
Chapter 3 holds together by a household. The Greek word for house recurs at the centre of each section: the overseer must 'manage his own household well,' verse 4, and if he cannot, 'how can he care for the church of God?' verse 5. The deacon must be a good manager 'of his own household,' verse 12, and the whole chapter explains in verse 15 'how each one must conduct himself in God's household.' What the leader is at home, he will be in the church, and the church itself is the larger house.

The overseer's list opens with a heading and then spells it out. 'Above reproach' sits first, and the items that follow fill it in. Almost every item is a question of character, appetite, temper, money, marriage, home and reputation. Only one is about skill, 'able to teach.' The overseer list also has a frame of warning at its end: the devil appears at verse 6 and again at verse 7, with the 'condemnation' and the 'snare' that wait for the proud or the disgraced.

The deacons are introduced by 'likewise,' and the same word returns at verse 11 for 'the women.' Each time Paul is saying that the same sort of person is needed here too. Verse 10 adds a step that verse 2 lacks, a period of testing before service.

Verses 14 and 15 are a pivot in which Paul states his purpose in the whole letter, and the passage then rises into an elevated six line confession in verse 16. The lines come in three pairs, each moving between two realms, flesh and Spirit, angels and nations, world and glory. Every verb in the hymn is in the same passive form. Nothing is said about what the church does; the whole confession is about what was done to and for the Son.
context.historical:
When Paul wrote, the churches of the Aegean were young and their leadership was still taking shape. The terms overseer and elder appear to refer to the same people. Paul called the Ephesian elders to Miletus and told them the Spirit had made them 'overseers,' Acts 20:17 and 28, and he told Titus to 'appoint elders' and then described what 'an overseer' must be, Titus 1:5 to 7. Peter, an elder himself, tells elders to 'be shepherds of God's flock,' 1 Peter 5:1 and 2. Philippians 1:1 greets 'the overseers and deacons.' A deacon is simply a servant. The seven men chosen in Acts 6:1 to 6 to look after the distribution to widows exercised that kind of service, and Phoebe is called a servant of the church in Cenchrea, Romans 16:1.

The standards named were readable by outsiders, which is why verse 7 insists on a good reputation 'with outsiders.' Roman society viewed new associations with suspicion, and a church whose leader was known as a drunkard, a brawler or a swindler would confirm every rumour. Hospitality mattered because travelling teachers and believers depended on private homes, and the churches met in houses, so an overseer's own household was in practice the church's meeting place.

The marriage language reflects a world where divorce and remarriage were easy and a man's household might include many dependants. A leader's home life was a public matter.

The hymn of verse 16 belongs to the church's earliest worship. Roughly a half century later the Roman governor Pliny reported that Christians in Bithynia met before dawn and sang to Christ as to a god. Verse 16 is the sort of song they were singing, a creed set to rhythm. In Ephesus, with its great temple of Artemis, a confession that the only revealed mystery is a person who appeared in the flesh was a deliberate rival to the local cult.
context.canonical:
The qualifications for overseers belong with Titus 1:5 to 9, where Paul gives a closely parallel list, adding that the overseer must 'hold firmly to the faithful word' so as to encourage with sound teaching and to refute opponents. Peter's counsel to elders to shepherd the flock 'not out of greed, but out of eagerness,' 1 Peter 5:2, matches 1 Timothy 3:3's 'free of the love of money.' Ezekiel 34:2 to 4 gives the warning in reverse, the shepherds who fed themselves and ruled with violence, and the lists in the Pastorals read like the remedy.

For deacons, Acts 6:1 to 6 shows a need being met by Spirit filled men of good standing, and Philippians 1:1 places overseers and deacons together. Jesus is the pattern of service: 'I am among you as one who serves,' Luke 22:27.

The picture of the church as God's household and temple runs through the New Testament. Ephesians 2:19 to 22 calls believers 'members of God's household' built into a holy temple, 1 Corinthians 3:16 says 'you yourselves are God's temple,' and Hebrews 3:5 and 6 contrasts Moses, faithful as a servant in God's house, with Christ as the Son over it. 'Pillar' is a word used of the leading apostles in Galatians 2:9 and of the faithful in Revelation 3:12.

The hymn is related to other early confessions. Romans 1:3 and 4 sets 'according to the flesh' beside 'through the Spirit of holiness,' Philippians 2:6 to 11 traces descent and exaltation, Colossians 1:15 to 20 celebrates the Son, and 1 Peter 3:18 and 22 speaks of being 'made alive in the Spirit' and going into heaven. The word 'mystery' is Paul's term for the plan hidden for ages and now made known, Romans 16:25 and 26, Ephesians 3:3 to 9 and Colossians 2:2, where it is simply 'Christ.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wrote so that the church would choose its leaders by what they are before it chooses them by what they can do. He begins with an aspiration, 'If anyone aspires to be an overseer, he desires a noble task,' and means it kindly: wanting to lead is not suspect, so long as the person understands that the thing wanted is work, a task, not a rank to be enjoyed. The qualities that follow then work as a net that keeps ambition honest.

He also meant Timothy to see that the home is the proving ground. The test of verses 4 and 5 is not whether a man's children are flawless but whether he has shown, in the small and difficult setting of his own family, the patience, firmness and gentleness that a congregation will need. A man who is harsh at home will not become gentle in a meeting.

He intended that the church's reputation outside would be protected. The leader has to be thought well of by those who do not share the faith, and Paul gives the reason: the devil sets 'the snare' there. The church's witness can be ruined by the failures of its leaders.

Finally, he gives the reason for it all in verses 14 to 16. Careful order is not an end in itself. The church is the household of the living God and carries the truth about Christ as a pillar carries a roof. Leaders are chosen so that the truth confessed in verse 16 will be held up, believed and passed on without being embarrassed by the lives of those who teach it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The two lists are meant to be normative. They describe the character that the church should look for in anyone who leads or serves, and the apostle repeats them in nearly the same form in Titus 1. Where they name specific things, such as not being a drunkard or violent, the underlying principle, self-control and gentleness, is clearly lasting.

Not every detail reads the same way to every church. 'The husband of but one wife' has been understood in several ways, as the debate below explains, and the instruction that a leader be one whose children are under control is read by some as a requirement that the children be believers and by others as a requirement of a well run home. The lists are also not exhaustive. They omit gifts that the New Testament elsewhere associates with leaders, and they do not mention many virtues that every Christian should have. They are a sample of what Paul considers essential for those who will be looked to as examples.

The hymn of verse 16 is of a different kind. It is not a command at all. It is a confession of what happened, and its purpose is to be believed, sung and taught. The chapter's application is to hold the two together: churches that insist on character in their leaders because they confess the Christ of verse 16.

Verse 11 about 'the women' is a description of whom Paul had in mind that readers have understood differently, as the second debate shows. Whichever way it is read, it is plain that the church's service includes women of dignity and trustworthiness.

debates.question: What does 'the husband of but one wife' require?

views.label: Not a polygamist
views.case: The phrase is read as excluding a man with more than one wife at once. Polygamy was practised by some in the ancient world, and a church leader was to model a single covenant. Many see this as the simplest sense of the words.

views.label: Not remarried after divorce, or after a spouse's death
views.case: Others read it as limiting leaders to men who have had only one wife in their lifetime. They point to 1 Timothy 5:9, which describes an enrolled widow as 'the wife of one man,' and think the same measure of marital history applies. Paul elsewhere permits remarriage for widows, so this reading has to explain why leaders would be held to a stricter standard.

views.label: Faithful to his wife
views.case: The literal phrase is 'a one woman man,' and the BSB footnote offers 'faithful to his wife.' On this reading the requirement is about fidelity and an undivided heart, whatever the man's marital past.

views.label: A norm that does not require marriage
views.case: Some add that the phrase describes the married man and does not disqualify a single leader. Paul himself was unmarried, 1 Corinthians 7:7 and 8, and no one doubts that he was a model for the churches' leaders.

debates.bearing: All views agree that sexual faithfulness is essential. The views differ on how to treat the marital past and on whether the singles are excluded, so churches have to apply the text with pastoral care and with the aim of seeing the same qualities of integrity.

debates.question: Who are 'the women' of verse 11?

views.label: Women who serve as deacons
views.case: The verse begins 'in the same way,' as verse 8 did, and it sits in the middle of the deacon section. Phoebe is called a diakonos in Romans 16:1. Verse 11 gives the women qualifications that parallel the men's, and no qualifications are given for the wives of overseers, which would be odd if wives were meant here.

views.label: The wives of deacons
views.case: The Greek word can mean either 'women' or 'wives,' and the BSB footnote offers 'their wives.' Some think Paul is describing the spouses whose conduct shapes a deacon's work. Verse 12 goes on to speak of a deacon's own wife and household.

views.label: Women who assist the deacons
views.case: A few suggest a recognised group of women helpers who were not strictly office holders.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle the question, and whichever reading is held, the qualities listed, dignity, truthfulness, sobriety and faithfulness, are the same ones required of all who serve.

debates.question: What does verse 16 say about the Spirit and about Christ's identity?

views.label: A creed of Christ's earthly and heavenly career
views.case: The six lines trace his appearing in flesh, his vindication, his being seen, proclaimed, believed and taken up. 'Vindicated by the Spirit' is then understood as the Spirit's raising and declaring him righteous, as in Romans 1:4 and 8:11.

views.label: A contrast between two spheres
views.case: The BSB footnote offers 'vindicated in spirit.' On this reading the lines set the earthly realm against the heavenly, flesh and spirit, in the pattern of 1 Peter 3:18, and the point is the transition from humiliation to exaltation.

views.label: A hymn arranged by place rather than by time
views.case: Some think the lines are not chronological and group earthly and heavenly events in pairs, so that 'seen by angels' refers to heavenly witness at the resurrection and ascension, not an earlier moment.

debates.bearing: All agree that the hymn confesses the incarnate, vindicated and glorified Lord. The footnote also records that some ancient manuscripts read 'God appeared,' and the BSB follows the reading 'He who appeared,' which many textual scholars favour.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb translated 'aspires' in verse 1 is oregomai, which means to stretch out the hand toward something. The same verb appears in 1 Timothy 6:10, where people 'craving' money wander from the faith, and in Hebrews 11:16, where the patriarchs desire a better country. So the stretching itself is neutral, and the object decides whether it is noble or ruinous. The 'task' that Paul commends is ergon, work, and the adjective kalon speaks of something fine and worthwhile. He is describing a labour worth wanting.

The word for 'hospitable,' philoxenos, is made of 'love' and 'stranger,' so it means a lover of strangers. Hebrews 13:2 tells all believers not to neglect it, and Titus 1:8 repeats it for overseers. 'Temperate' is nephalios, literally sober or clear-headed, and Paul uses it again of the women in verse 11 and of older men in Titus 2:2. The picture is of someone whose judgment is not clouded.

The verb in verses 4, 5 and 12 for managing, proistemi, literally means to stand before, and so to lead or to preside. In verse 5 it is paired with epimeleomai, 'care for,' the verb Jesus uses of the Samaritan who took the wounded man to an inn and said 'take care of him,' Luke 10:34 and 35. Leading and caring are placed side by side: the one who stands in front is the one who bends down.

In verse 8 'double-tongued' is dilogos, saying one thing to one person and another thing to the next. Verse 6's 'conceited' is typhoo, from a word for smoke, and means to be puffed up or clouded by pride. Paul uses it again of the false teacher in 1 Timothy 6:4.

Verse 11 plays on a word. Women must not be 'slanderers,' which is the plural of diabolos, the word that in verses 6 and 7 is the name of the devil. The word means one who accuses or throws accusations, so the devil is the slanderer by trade, and a believer who spreads slander is doing his work. Titus 2:3 says the same of older women.

'Tested' in verse 10 is dokimazo, the verb for proving metal or approving a coin as genuine, and it is the same family as Paul's 'approved' in 1 Thessalonians 2:4.

The hymn's verbs are worth noticing. 'Appeared' is ephanerothe, to make visible what was hidden. 'Was seen' is ophthe, the verb that 1 Corinthians 15:5 to 8 uses for each appearance of the risen Lord, so 'seen by angels' places angels among those who witnessed him. 'Was vindicated' is edikaiothe, from the word for righteousness, and carries a legal sense of being declared right. 'Was taken up' is anelemphthe, the verb Acts 1:11 uses of the ascension.

typology.type: The household and its pillars, verses 4 to 5 and 15
typology.fulfillment: In Israel, God's dwelling was a tent and then a temple whose entrance was marked by two named pillars, Jachin and Boaz, 1 Kings 7:21. Moses was 'faithful as a servant in all God's house,' but Christ is 'faithful as the Son over God's house,' Hebrews 3:5 and 6, and Paul can say believers are 'God's temple,' 1 Corinthians 3:16, and 'members of God's household,' Ephesians 2:19. The church is therefore the true house whose pillar carries the truth. The type falls short because stone pillars supported a building; the church supports the truth by living and confessing it.

The overseer's character answers the failure of Israel's shepherds in Ezekiel 34:2 to 4, who fed themselves and ruled with violence. Moses was given elders to share the burden of the people, Numbers 11:16 and 17. In the new covenant, elders are told to shepherd God's flock, 1 Peter 5:2, under the 'Chief Shepherd,' 1 Peter 5:4. The fulfilment is Jesus, the shepherd whose care the leaders imitate. The pattern falls short because every human overseer is himself one of the flock, and the lists are needed precisely because leaders can fail.

The seven chosen in Acts 6 served at tables so the apostles could attend to prayer and the word, and Paul's deacons follow the same pattern of humble, practical service. Jesus is the fulfilment of the pattern, since he said, 'I am among you as one who serves,' Luke 22:27, and that he came 'to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. A deacon's standing grows with faithful service, verse 13, but the pattern of service finds its measure in the cross.

Enoch 'walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away,' Genesis 5:24, and Elijah 'went up into heaven in a whirlwind,' 2 Kings 2:11. Both anticipate a human being received into the presence of God. Christ's ascension goes further, since he is taken up to sit at God's right hand, Psalm 110:1, in glory, and he will return in the same way, Acts 1:11. The older figures were taken to heaven without a work accomplished for others; he is taken up as the one who finished a work of redemption.

study.christ:
The chapter closes with Christ in six lines, and everything before it has been preparing for that. 'He appeared in the flesh' states the incarnation in the plainest terms. The Son who existed before was made visible, as John 1:14 says, 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us.' Paul calls the whole thing 'the mystery of godliness,' meaning that the secret of a godly life is not a technique but a person. Colossians 2:2 and 3 says the mystery is 'Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.'

'Vindicated by the Spirit' says that the one who was condemned and crucified was declared right. Romans 1:4 says he was 'declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead,' and Romans 4:25 that he 'was raised to life for our justification.' The cross looked like a verdict against him, and the resurrection reversed it.

'Seen by angels' reaches into the unseen world. Heaven's creatures watched him at his birth, his testing, his rising and his ascending. 1 Peter 1:12 says that 'even angels long to look into these things,' and Hebrews 1:6 shows them worshipping when God brings his firstborn into the world. What is plain to us as a story is a matter of wonder to them.

'Proclaimed among the nations' and 'believed in throughout the world' announce the gospel's movement across every boundary, and they fulfil what Jesus commanded in Matthew 28:19. The mystery once kept hidden is now made known to the Gentiles, Ephesians 3:3 to 9. The last line, 'taken up in glory,' ends with the ascension, and it is worth noticing that the hymn does not climax with the cross or the empty tomb alone but with exaltation.

The chapter also bears on Christ in what it asks of leaders. Every item on the overseer's list is a feature of the one who is Chief Shepherd. He is 'without sin,' Hebrews 4:15, and 'No deceit was found in His mouth,' 1 Peter 2:22, which is the fullness of 'above reproach.' He was rich and 'became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9, which is the opposite of the love of money. He was tested in every way, Hebrews 4:15, though not found wanting, which gives meaning to the testing of deacons. He was faithful to his bride and gave himself up for her to present her 'holy and blameless,' Ephesians 5:25 to 27, which stands behind 'the husband of but one wife.' The leader's character is a small copy of the one he serves.

A caution is in order. Verse 16 is explicit about Christ, but the lists of qualifications are not code for him. They show his character only in the sense that all Christian virtue does.
study.god:
The most striking word about God in this chapter is the title in verse 15, 'the living God.' It is a title with a history. The Old Testament contrasts the living God with idols that cannot see or speak, and the apostles use it in the same way. Paul told the people of Lystra to turn from worthless things 'to the living God, who made heaven and earth,' Acts 14:15, and wrote to the Thessalonians that they had turned 'from idols to serve the living and true God,' 1 Thessalonians 1:9. In Ephesus, where silversmiths shouted 'Great is Artemis of the Ephesians,' Acts 19:28, the claim that the church belongs to the living God was a confession set against the city's most visible worship.

The chapter also shows a God who owns a household and cares how it is run. The house is his, and those who lead in it are stewards. Titus 1:7 says so openly, 'As God's steward, an overseer must be above reproach.' This explains the weight placed on character. The leader acts for someone else, and the owner's honour is at stake. God is not satisfied with leaders who are merely effective.

He is the God of truth who has made the church the keeper of what he has revealed. The 'pillar and foundation of the truth' does not mean the church creates truth; it means the church holds it up before the world, as a pillar holds up a roof. The truth itself is God's revealing, the mystery 'kept hidden in God, who created all things,' Ephesians 3:9, and now made known.

The hymn shows God the Father acting toward his Son. The vindication, the taking up in glory, and the believing of the nations are things done to the Son by the Father through the Spirit, so the passage has a threefold shape without needing to say so. The same God who hid the mystery for ages has now brought it into the light.

He is also the God who tests and approves. The tested deacons of verse 10 reflect the way God examines hearts, as 1 Thessalonians 2:4 puts it, and the reputation among outsiders shows that he cares what the world sees of his people.

For worship, the passage invites the church to sing its confession. A creed set to music teaches the doctrine of the incarnation in a form that a whole congregation can hold. Worship that begins with the greatness of the mystery will also find it easier to value leaders of honest character, since both belong to the household of the living God.

crossReferences.note: A parallel list of qualifications for elders and overseers, set down for a church in Crete. Comparing the two lists shows what Paul regarded as essential, and shows that elder and overseer describe the same role.

Paul tells the Ephesian elders that the Holy Spirit has made them overseers and calls them to shepherd the church of God. It shows the two titles used for the same people in the same city where Timothy is working.

Seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom are chosen to serve the widows so the apostles can devote themselves to prayer and the word. It is the clearest early example of the kind of service that gave rise to the deacons.

Paul greets the saints at Philippi together with the overseers and deacons. It shows the two offices existing side by side in an established church, written well before this letter perhaps, and so confirms the picture that 1 Timothy 3 draws of both groups.
Peter urges elders to shepherd willingly, eagerly and without greed, and to be examples, with the Chief Shepherd's crown in view. It matches the heart of the overseer's list and gives it a motive.
God condemns shepherds who feed themselves and rule with violence while the flock goes hungry. It stands behind the insistence that overseers be gentle and free from the love of money.
Believers are members of God's household, built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, and growing into a holy temple. It explains what Paul means in 3:15 by the household of God.

Moses was a faithful servant in God's house, but Christ is faithful as the Son over God's house, and 'we are His house.' It shows that the household language of 1 Timothy 3:15 carries the weight of the whole story of God's dwelling.

Another early hymn tracing the descent of Christ and his exaltation to the name above every name. It parallels the movement of 1 Timothy 3:16 from humility to glory, and shows that confessing the whole career of Christ in rhythmic lines was a settled habit of the early churches.

Christ is descended from David 'according to the flesh' and declared Son of God 'through the Spirit of holiness' by the resurrection. It sets flesh beside Spirit as 1 Timothy 3:16 does and shows the same early pattern of confession.
The disciples watch Jesus taken up and are told that he will come back the same way. It is the narrative behind the last line of the hymn, 'taken up in glory.'

The mystery hidden for ages is made known through the gospel, so that the Gentiles are fellow heirs. It explains what Paul means by 'mystery' and why the hymn speaks of Christ proclaimed among the nations.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning God has dwelt among a people and set leaders over them. In Eden he walked with the man and woman. In the wilderness he lived in a tent among Israel and appointed elders to share the burden of Moses, Numbers 11:16 and 17. In Jerusalem he filled a temple whose pillars stood at its door. The question that runs through all of it is who may serve in his presence, and what kind of person they must be. 1 Timothy 3 gives the answer for the age of the church.

The story has shown again and again how leaders can fail. Eli's sons took what was not theirs, the kings of Judah led the people astray, and Ezekiel's shepherds fed themselves while the flock starved. The lists of this chapter are the church's answer to that history, a set of marks by which a congregation can recognise a person who will not repeat it. They look forward to the day when God himself will shepherd his people, as he promised in Ezekiel 34, and in Christ he has.

The church is now the household and temple of the living God. The prophets spoke of a day when God would dwell among his people, and Paul says that his dwelling is now the gathered believers, built together in the Spirit, Ephesians 2:22. The 'pillar and foundation of the truth' carries a calling that Israel had as a light to the nations, now given to a people drawn from all nations.

The hymn of verse 16 traces the story of Christ from his appearing to his glory, and it sums up the plot of the Bible in a line. The hidden mystery is revealed, the one who was rejected is vindicated, the nations believe, and the Lord is taken up. What remains is his return, which Acts 1:11 promises.

The story ends in a household without any need of a pillar. Revelation 21:3 hears a voice from the throne, 'the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.' There will be elders around the throne, Revelation 4:4, and the saints will be priests to God, Revelation 1:6, and the character shaped in them now will be complete. Until then, the church needs overseers and deacons who show something of the Shepherd and the Servant they follow, and it needs the confession of verse 16 to remind it who the Lord is.

quiz.q: What does Paul emphasize most in the qualifications for overseers?

options.text: Proven, above-reproach character, with the ability to teach.
options.note: The list is dominated by character, with able to teach the one functional trait, verses 2 and 3.

options.text: A commanding personality and large following.
options.note: He must teach, but the stress falls on character, not charisma.

options.text: Wealth and high social rank.
options.note: Paul warns the overseer must be free of the love of money.

options.text: Many years of formal schooling.
options.note: The focus is godly character and aptness to teach, not diplomas.

quiz.q: Why must an overseer manage his own household well?

options.text: Because one who cannot manage his home cannot care for the church of God.
options.note: Verse 5 draws this direct line from home to church.

options.text: Because family size proves a man's worth.
options.note: The point is faithful management, not the number of children.

options.text: Because the church is unrelated to home life.
options.note: Paul ties the two closely; the home is a proving ground.

options.text: Because only wealthy households qualify.
options.note: It is about management and character, not wealth.

quiz.q: What must deacons hold to, according to verse 9?

options.text: The mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.
options.note: Verse 9 names this as the deacon's inner requirement.

options.text: A secret teaching known only to leaders.
options.note: The mystery is revealed truth to be confessed, not a hidden secret.

options.text: Their own personal opinions.
options.note: They hold the faith once delivered, not private ideas.

options.text: Nothing in particular; only practical skills matter.
options.note: Character and holding the faith are both required.

quiz.q: What does Paul call the church in verse 15?

options.text: The household of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.
options.note: Verse 15 gives this description of the church.

options.text: A human club with no divine calling.
options.note: It is the household of the living God, not a mere club.

options.text: The source that invents new truth.
options.note: The church upholds the truth; it does not create it.

options.text: An optional add-on to the Christian life.
options.note: Paul treats the church as central, the pillar of the truth.

quiz.q: What is the mystery of godliness confessed in verse 16?

options.text: Christ appeared in the flesh, was vindicated, and was taken up in glory.
options.note: Verse 16 rehearses the gospel of the incarnate and exalted Christ.

options.text: A hidden ritual open only to the initiated.
options.note: The mystery is revealed and openly confessed, not a private rite.

options.text: The secret to worldly success and wealth.
options.note: It concerns Christ and salvation, not earthly gain.

options.text: That godliness cannot really be known.
options.note: The mystery is revealed in Christ and proclaimed to the nations.

questions: Paul chooses leaders by tested character before gifting. When you look to whom you follow, how much weight do you give to proven godliness?
The overseer's home life is a proving ground for church care. What does the way you handle your closest relationships reveal about your readiness to serve others?
Deacons must first be tested. Where in your life is God testing your faithfulness in small things before entrusting you with more?
The church is the pillar and foundation of the truth. How seriously do you take your part in a local church that upholds and displays the gospel?
The mystery of godliness is the story of Christ from flesh to glory. Which line of that confession most stirs your worship today, and why?

translationNotes.note: The husband of but one wife renders a phrase meaning a one-woman man; the BSB footnote offers faithful to his wife, stressing marital fidelity, and applies also in verse 12.
The women here can be rendered their wives, as the footnote notes, leaving open whether Paul means women deacons or the wives of deacons.
He appeared follows the earliest reading, literally He who appeared; the footnote records the later reading God appeared, behind the King James; both confess the incarnate Christ.
